newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German leaders quiet on French EMU worries.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German leaders quiet on French EMU worries.

text.p: German politicians showed a marked reluctance on Tuesday to comment on France's battle to qualify for the single European currency despite continued uncertainty over whether Paris can make the grade so the project can start on schedule.
For the second time in the past few days, Finance Minister Theo Waigel sidestepped a question about whether Paris could meet the entry criteria for economic and monetary union (EMU).

Waigel told a news conference in Berlin that all countries, including France, had agreed everyone must do their own homework. "We're doing that and so are others," he said. "I'm not evaluating the efforts of others."

Even Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber, a fierce advocate of strictly interpreting the criteria, appeared to hold his fire while Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel hinted strongly he favoured exploiting room for manoeuvre in the Maastricht Treaty.

France's Socialist-led government has raised doubts about its ability to meet the fiscal criteria for the single currency, particularly the budget deficit target of three percent of gross domestic product.
German jitters can hardly have been eased by President Jacques Chirac, who said on Monday France was running a budget deficit of around 3.5 percent of GDP.

If Paris were to miss the target, Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government would be left with a choice of postponing the project or agreeing not to interpret "three percent" as exactly 3.0, independent economists have said.

But Waigel resisted the temptation to comment on France specifically, saying the decision on EMU members would only be taken when official statistics for the whole of 1997 were available, probably next March.
"There are clear targets and clear agreements," he said. "Every country has the chance and the obligation to do their bit in 1997 to meet the criteria."
Waigel also declined to comment last week at a Bonn news conference when he was asked about France's chances.

Stoiber told Berlin broadcaster Inforadio there was little point working with predictions and that everything depended on the official statistics, although he also reiterated his stance that three percent must mean 3.0 for everyone.

"You certainly can't build a common European house if some people build walls of stone and, so to speak, they're using papier-mache on the other side -- that certainly wouldn't be a stable home," he said.
Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel, however, appeared to advocate using the leeway in the treaty when it came to the criteria.

"I have always been opposed to the decimal point discussion. People should just take a look at what is in the Maastricht Treaty. What is written there is what is required," Kinkel said in an interview with the Neue Osnabruecker Zeitung daily.

Asked if this meant three did not have to mean 3.0, Kinkel simply replied: "Everyone who is talking about figures at the moment should be aware of their responsibility. That is why I refer to the articles of the treaty."
